title: Is This a Movement (Only) for Moms?
author: Leah Libresco Sargeant
summary: Leah Libresco Sargeant answers a critique from The Argument's gender reporter, who asked whether a women's movement rooted in biology becomes reductionist and narrow. She replies that pregnancy is the starkest sex asymmetry and an obvious route to solidarity, but that she cares about every asymmetry, from height and hand size to hormonal cycles and a built world designed with men as the default. Drawing on her book The Dignity of Dependence, she argues that culture wrongly grounds the equal dignity of men and women in interchangeability and sets an unreachable ideal of autonomy for both sexes. Pregnancy and early childcare often expose that lie for women, while men tend to discover their dependence later through aging, illness, or injury. She insists her feminism does not make motherhood every woman's destiny, and that single and childless people have especially fragile claims to care and need deliberate inclusion. The post closes with a short exchange on how the virtues of a high-stakes career carry over to parenting.
points: The pregnancy asymmetry is the clearest route into solidarity among women, but Libresco Sargeant stresses it is only one of many sex differences, including drug dosing, tool sizes, and crash-test design.
Grounding dignity in interchangeability makes the claim to equal dignity fragile, since men and women are not fully interchangeable.
The cultural ideal of autonomy fails both sexes because everyone begins and ends life dependent and relies on others in between.
Care that is not tied to an obvious biological bond, such as that owed to single and childless people, tends to be treated as optional unless communities deliberately include them.
Her practical example is choosing single or infertile friends as godparents, creating a permanent relationship of love and obligation.
quotes: The asymmetry of pregnancy is the most obvious difference between men and women, but it isn’t the only important distinction. Women are biologically different from men, and that shows up in our heights, our hand size, our hormonal cycles, whether you ever have a baby or not.

You don’t have to have children to be endangered or inconvenienced as a woman by drugs that ignore your hormonal cycles, tools the wrong size for your hands, or an airbag that was never calibrated with a female-sized crash test dummy.

First, our culture often premises the equal dignity of men and women on our interchangeability. (But since men and women aren’t fully interchangeable, our claim to dignity, at least through that route, is fragile.)
We begin our lives obviously dependent, we end our lives the same way, and we spend a great deal of the time in between relying on others.
For women, pregnancy is often the tipping point: While you’re pregnant or caring for a very young child, it’s more obvious that you can’t live up to the ideal of autonomy.

The nursing mother is less free to sit by the bedside of her dying father than the single woman. The man in a religious order has already chosen a form of laying down his life, and does not have to weigh whether a war is just and whether he owes it to his nation and his neighbors to enlist.
Persons who are single are freer to make sudden commitments in a crisis, but also are more likely to struggle to find someone committed to them in their crisis.
